extracted.intended_audience: literate English readers, aspiring writers, journalists, and educators (early-18th-century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Short satirical essays giving practical and moral advice about language use, clarity in reporting, responsibilities of authors, imagination vs. reason, pedagogy, and public manners for writers and commentators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language purity — oppose foreign phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have often wished, that ... certain Men might be set apart as Superintendants of our Language, to hinder any Words of a Foreign Coin from passing among us; and in particular to prohibit any French Phrases from becoming Current in this Kingdom... The present War has so Adulterated our Tongue with strange Words...","The French would indeed be in the right to publish the News of the present War in English Phrases...","The Histories of all our former Wars are transmitted to us in our Vernacular Idiom..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: guard the mother-tongue against importation of foreign phrases when native words will do; appoint figurative 'superintendents' of language. Example/anti-pattern: military/news accounts littered with French terms learned from conquered enemies (e.g., 'Gens d'Arms', 'Charte Blanche', 'Gasconade') that render reports unintelligible to ordinary readers. Scoring note: prefer 'our own Stamp' words where clarity and national self-understanding are at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity in reportage — use plain English to describe actions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The English cannot be too clear in their Narrative of those Actions... and which will be still the more admired the better they are explained."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: when reporting events (especially wars), choose plain, vernacular expressions rather than technical or foreign jargon. Illustrative failure: a soldier's report that so uses terms of art that his father and the parish curate cannot tell what news it contains. Remedy: translate technical phrases into accessible language; employ secretaries or clear exposition to communicate deeds to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility of authors — avoid corrupting posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: "How careful should an Author be of committing any thing to Print that may corrupt Posterity, and poison the Minds of Men with Vice and Error? Writers of great Talents, who employ their Parts in propagating Immorality, and seasoning vicious Sentiments with Wit and Humour, are to be looked upon as the Pests of Society..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: authors should weigh the ethical effects and long-term influence of their publications; avoid cloaking immoral or corrupting ideas with wit. Example/anecdote: story of an atheistical author who, on his sickbed, fears his writings will seduce future ages. Anti-pattern: producing clever but morally damaging tracts for transient fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the durability and legacy of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Books are the Legacies that a great Genius leaves to Mankind... This gives a great Author something like a Prospect of Eternity..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: remember that printed works can outlast other arts (statues, buildings, paintings) by being multiplied; therefore choose what you commit to print with regard to posterity. Practical implication: aim for substance and virtue, since copied writings become the enduring record of a mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance imagination with reason — avoid 'castle-building' that disconnects from reality
rubrics_metrics.description: "The unhappy Force of an Imagination, unguided by the Check of Reason and Judgment... A Castle-builder is ... who erects their Structures in the most unstable of Elements, the Air... the least Breath of Wind has often demolished my magnificent Edifices... The ill Consequence of these Reveries is inconceivably great..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: cultivate imagination but temper it with judgment and practical sense; excessive day-dreaming harms economy, coherence of thought, and real life performance. Anti-patterns: letting fancy supplant duties, producing incoherent diversity of thoughts, or suffering real losses because of imaginary investments. Suggested remedy: seek methods to ‘settle the head’ and restore balance between fancy and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not invent public falsehoods or force belief
rubrics_metrics.description: "The same ungoverned Fancy which pushed that Correspondent on, in spite of himself, to relate publick and notorious Falsehoods... makes the Author of the following Letter do the same in Private; one is a Prating, the other a Silent Liar."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: distinguish harmless fiction from presenting invented incidents as truth; avoid asserting false events in public narratives. Anti-pattern: embellishing plain narratives into falsehoods (prating) or privately living under false pretences (silent lying). Ethical note: truthfulness preserves an author's reputation and the public's trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization in satire — portray social types singly and in sets
rubrics_metrics.description: "You have represented several sorts of Impertinents singly, I wish you would now proceed, and describe some of them in Sets... Sometimes you have a Set of Whisperers... sometimes a Set of Laughers... You frequently meet with these Sets at the Opera, the Play..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: when satirizing or depicting manners, consider grouping characters whose impertinences act in concert; depict the dynamics of sets (whisperers, laughers, etc.) to illustrate social patterns. Example: describe how a small party can distract a whole assembly. Anti-pattern: treating such behavior only as isolated quirks rather than patterned social types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogy and tone of instruction — make learning pleasurable and humane
rubrics_metrics.description: "We might then possibly see Learning become a Pleasure, and Children delighting themselves in that which now they abhor... It is a worthy Attempt to undertake the Cause of distrest Youth... that those who Disturb others should pay at least a double Price..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: teachers should be polite and use humane methods rather than corporal severity; pedagogy that makes learning pleasurable produces genuine scholars and prevents pedantry. Anti-patterns: severe schoolmasters who terrify children and break spirited minds; remedy: place courteous, methodical instructors above parental influence and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict and enforce public decency — critique disruptive behavior in assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: "For preserving therefore the Decency of publick Assemblies, methinks it would be but reasonable that those who Disturb others should pay at least a double Price for their Places... Women of Birth... should be informed that a Levity of Behaviour ... degrades them below their meanest Attendants..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: in essays and social commentary, call out manners that disturb public entertainments (opera, theatre, water-works); propose sanctions (higher price, social admonition) and stress that clothing/status without comportment is hollow. Illustrative anti-pattern: people of fortune adopting footmen-like manners; remedy: public and social pressure toward decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete anecdotes and letters as illustrative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The page repeatedly uses stories, letters, and anecdotes (e.g., the Blenheim army-letter, the dying atheist, Theodosius/Constantia) to make points and persuade readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: support abstract moral or stylistic claims with vivid, concrete examples and short narrative extracts. Benefit: makes criticism memorable and shows real-world implications. Anti-pattern: abstract moralizing without exemplification, which fails to persuade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: blend moral instruction with wit and satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the papers the author combines moral admonition with humour, elegancy, and satirical portraiture (e.g., gentle reproof of writers who corrupt, playful mockery of 'castle-builders').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: adopt a style that delivers ethical or social critique lightly—use wit and elegant phrasing to engage readers while still conveying seriousness. Anti-pattern: heavy-handed moralizing that alienates readers, or wit without a moral centre that trivializes important points.
